rationale: Jesus introduces the words by naming the prophet ("Isaiah prophesied correctly about you," 15:7, BSB) and then quotes Isaiah 29:13, which is why the type is quotation and the label is explicit, following conn-matt13-hardening-isaiah6. The formula is not one of Matthew's "to fulfill" formulas; in Matthew's BSB the verb "prophesied" occurs only here and at 11:13. Checked in this app's BSB, Isaiah 29:13 reads "These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men," and Matthew 15:8-9 reads "These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men." The last line is where Matthew follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew. The Hebrew, glossed word by word on Bible Hub's interlinear, reads "and is," "their reverence," "toward Me," "a commandment," "by men," "taught"; it has no word for "in vain." The Septuagint as Bible Hub serves it reads matēn de sebontai me didaskontes entalmata anthrōpōn kai didaskalias (Brenton: "but in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men"), and every Greek edition of Matthew 15:9 listed on Bible Hub reads matēn de sebontai me, didaskontes didaskalias entalmata anthrōpōn: the Septuagint's words, with "doctrines" moved forward and "and" dropped. The first line splits by edition: the SBL, Nestle 1904, Westcott-Hort and Tischendorf texts omit "draw near to Me with their mouth," which both the Hebrew and the Septuagint have, while the Byzantine, Greek Orthodox and both Textus Receptus texts include it (Engizei moi ... tō stomati autōn). Ellicott (via Bible Hub) says the quotation "is given substantially from the Greek version"; the Cambridge Bible says it "does not follow precisely either the LXX. version or the Hebrew text." In Isaiah the words concern "These people" of "the city of Ariel where David camped" (29:1, BSB); how a prophecy to Isaiah's generation is "about" Jesus' questioners is read differently by Calvin and Barnes (see the lesson). The same quotation stands in Mark 7:6-7, which is covered by the Mark row, not a separate Isaiah row.
